arXiv:2605.29151v1 [math.AG] 27 May 2026

Real-Rootedness of the Poincaré polynomials of ℳ¯0,n\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n}:
an AI-assisted proof

Gergely Bérczi and Young-Hoon Kiem Address: Department of Mathematics, Aarhus University, Ny Munkegade 118, 8000 Aarhus, Denmark Email address: gergely.berczi@math.au.dk Address: School of Mathematics, Korea Institute for Advanced Study, 85 Hoegiro, Dongdaemun-gu, Seoul 02455, Korea Email address: kiem@kias.re.kr
Abstract.

We prove the real-rootedness for the Poincaré polynomial

Pn​(t)=∑i=0n−3dimH2​i​(ℳ¯0,n,ℚ)​tiP_{n}(t)=\sum_{i=0}^{n-3}\dim H^{2i}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n};\mathbb{Q})t^{i}

of the Deligne–Mumford moduli space ℳ¯0,n\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n} of stable nn-pointed rational curves, proving a conjecture of Aluffi–Chen–Marcolli.

The proof starts from the Keel–Manin–Getzler recurrence for these polynomials, but its main new idea is the introduction of a bivariate deformation Fm​(y,t)F_{m}(y,t) of the Poincaré polynomial. This deformation is the heart of the argument: it reveals a hidden interlacing structure which is not visible from the one-variable recurrence alone. For fixed t<0t<0, the zero set of FmF_{m} in the yy-direction is governed by a Sturm–Rolle argument on the interval 0<y<1−t0<y<1-t. The original polynomial Pn​(t)P_{n}(t) is recovered by the slice y=1y=1, and the ordered crossings of the moving roots through this slice give both real-rootedness and strict interlacing. As a consequence, the Betti numbers of ℳ¯0,n\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n} form an ultra-log-concave sequence. We further show the real-rootedness and ultra-log-concavity for the Poincaré polynomial of the Fulton-MacPherson space ℙ1​[n]\mathbb{P}^{1}[n] of nn ordered points in (degenerations of) the complex projective line ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}.

The proof of the real-rootedness theorem for the Poincaré polynomials of ℳ¯0,n\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n} was obtained through an iterative AI-assisted workflow with Co-Mathematician, an agentic frontier-model system developed by Google DeepMind [ZvGZ+26]. The human role was to pose the problem, evaluate the mathematical plausibility of successive attempts, identify and request repairs of gaps, compare the evolving argument with the literature, and assemble the final human-verifiable proof. Our additional human contribution was to observe that a similar, residual deformation strategy also applies to the Fulton–MacPherson spaces ℙ1​[n]\mathbb{P}^{1}[n], which yields the corresponding real-rootedness theorem.

1. Introduction

The Deligne–Mumford moduli spaces are central geometric objects of modern algebraic geometry. Deligne and Mumford introduced stable curves and their moduli space ℳ¯g\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g} in their 1969 paper [DM69]. The pointed compactifications ℳ¯g,n\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g,n}, including the genus-zero spaces considered in the present paper, were constructed in the Grothendieck–Knudsen theory of stable pointed curves [Knu83a, Knu83b]. The space ℳ¯0,n\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n} is a smooth projective variety of dimension n−3n-3 compactifying configurations of nn ordered points on the complex projective line ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} modulo projective equivalence. The importance of these moduli spaces comes from their rich geometry which has led to several complementary discoveries. First, the boundary, forgetful, and clutching morphisms relating the spaces ℳ¯g,n\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g,n} organize them into the basic geometric framework for stable curve theory. In particular, the so-called clutching morphisms encode the fundamental operation of gluing pointed curves along marked points, an operation which gives the collection of moduli spaces its operadic, and in higher genus modular operadic, structure [GK98]. In genus zero, Keel computed the Chow ring and intersection theory of ℳ¯0,n\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n}, proving in particular the recursive structure of its Chow groups and Betti numbers [Kee92]. Kapranov then related ℳ¯0,n\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n} to explicit birational and combinatorial models, including iterated blow-ups, Veronese curves and Chow quotients of Grassmannians [Kap93]. In a different direction, Witten’s conjectural description of intersection numbers on moduli spaces of curves through two-dimensional gravity, and Kontsevich’s proof via the matrix Airy function, made ℳ¯g,n\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g,n} a central bridge between algebraic geometry, integrable systems and mathematical physics [Wit91, Kon92]. Kontsevich–Manin’s formulation of Gromov–Witten classes and quantum cohomology then placed stable curves and stable maps at the foundation of modern enumerative geometry [KM94]. More recently, the cohomology of ℳ¯0,n+1\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n+1} has been understood as a Chow ring attached to the braid matroid and the minimal building set, connecting these moduli spaces to matroid Chow rings and combinatorial Hodge theory [EFM+25, AHK18, FMSV24].

In this paper we study Betti numbers of ℳ¯0,n\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n}, encoded by the Poincaré polynomial (in half-degree convention)

(1) Pn​(t)=∑i=0n−3bn,i​ti,bn,i=dimH2​i​(ℳ¯0,n,ℚ).P_{n}(t)=\sum_{i=0}^{n-3}b_{n,i}t^{i},\qquad b_{n,i}=\dim H^{2i}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n};\mathbb{Q}).

The main result is a fundamental new structural property of the topology of these moduli spaces: for every n≥3n\geq 3, the Poincaré polynomial Pn​(t)P_{n}(t) has only real roots. The proof was found with the assistance of Co-Mathematician, a frontier agentic LLM-based system for mathematical research introduced in [ZvGZ+26].

Theorem 1.1.

For every n≥3n\geq 3, the polynomial Pn​(t)P_{n}(t) has only real roots. More precisely, for n≥4n\geq 4 it has n−3n-3 simple roots, all lying in (−∞,0)(-\infty,0).

We also obtain strict interlacing.

Theorem 1.2 (Strict interlacing).

Let n≥4n\geq 4, and let

τ1<τ2<⋯<τn−3<0\tau_{1}<\tau_{2}<\cdots<\tau_{n-3}<0

be the roots of Pn​(t)P_{n}(t). If

σ1<σ2<⋯<σn−2<0\sigma_{1}<\sigma_{2}<\cdots<\sigma_{n-2}<0

are the roots of Pn+1​(t)P_{n+1}(t), then

σ1<τ1<σ2<τ2<⋯<σn−3<τn−3<σn−2<0.\sigma_{1}<\tau_{1}<\sigma_{2}<\tau_{2}<\cdots<\sigma_{n-3}<\tau_{n-3}<\sigma_{n-2}<0.

Note that odd cohomology vanishes, and PnP_{n} is palindromic by Poincaré duality. Hard Lefschetz gives unimodality of the coefficients. Since the coefficients are nonnegative, the roots are necessarily negative; Newton’s inequalities then give log-concavity, indeed ultra-log-concavity, of the Betti number sequence.

Corollary 1.3 (Log-concavity of the Betti numbers).

For every n≥3n\geq 3, the Betti numbers of M¯0,n\overline{M}_{0,n} form an ultra-log-concave sequence:

(bn,i(n−3i))2≥bn,i−1(n−3i−1)​bn,i+1(n−3i+1)for all ​1≤i≤n−4.\left(\frac{b_{n,i}}{\binom{n-3}{i}}\right)^{2}\geq\frac{b_{n,i-1}}{\binom{n-3}{i-1}}\frac{b_{n,i+1}}{\binom{n-3}{i+1}}\qquad\text{for all }1\leq i\leq n-4.

A closely related space to ℳ¯0,n\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n} is the Fulton–MacPherson space ℙ1​[n]\mathbb{P}^{1}[n] which compactifies the configuration space of nn ordered distinct points in ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} without projective equivalence. It is a smooth projective variety of dimension nn with vanishing odd cohomology and its even Betti sequence is unimodal and palindromic. By the same technique as in the proof of Theorem 1.1, we further prove the real-rootedness (Theorem 5.1) and the ultra-log-concavity (Corollary 5.2) for the Poincaré polynomial of ℙ1​[n]\mathbb{P}^{1}[n] for n≥1n\geq 1.

We next recall the precise origin of the problem. Aluffi–Chen–Marcolli formulated the real-rootedness conjecture for the polynomial representing the Grothendieck class of ℳ¯0,n\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n}; in the Poincaré specialization this is exactly the assertion that Pn​(t)P_{n}(t) has only real zeros [ACM25, Conjecture 1]. They proved asymptotic ultra-log-concavity and γ\gamma-positivity as evidence for the conjecture. Nascimento improved the asymptotic ultra-log-concavity bounds [Nas25]. Aluffi–Marcolli–Nascimento gave explicit formulas for the Grothendieck class and Betti numbers in terms of Stirling and Bernoulli numbers, and verified related log-concavity phenomena in large finite ranges [AMN25]. Choi–Kiem–Lee first gave closed formulas for the 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n}-characters on cohomology, then developed recursive algorithms for these representations and proposed strong equivariant log-concavity refinements of the Betti number log-concavity problem; their later work introduced characteristic polynomials of representations and further asymptotic log-concavity results [CKL23, CKL24, CKL25]. Choi–Kiem later proved that the distribution of the Betti numbers of ℳ¯0,n\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n} is asymptotically Gaussian and obtained a stronger asymptotic ultra-log-concavity [CK26].

The recursion used in this paper is the standard recursion for the Betti numbers of ℳ¯0,n\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n}:

(2) P1​(t)=P2​(t)=P3​(t)=1,P_{1}(t)=P_{2}(t)=P_{3}(t)=1,

and, for n>3n>3,

(3) Pn​(t)=(1+t)​Pn−1​(t)+t​∑j=3n−2(n−2j−1)​Pj​(t)​Pn+1−j​(t).P_{n}(t)=(1+t)P_{n-1}(t)+t\sum_{j=3}^{n-2}\binom{n-2}{j-1}P_{j}(t)P_{n+1-j}(t).

This recurrence follows from Keel’s recursive construction and Chow ring computation [Kee92]; it is equivalent to generating function identities appearing in the work of Manin and Getzler [Man95, Get95]. We use (3) as our starting point.

The proof is not a direct manipulation of the coefficients of PnP_{n}. Its central idea is to lift the one-variable problem to a two-variable problem. We introduce polynomials Fm​(y,t)F_{m}(y,t) satisfying

(4) F1​(y,t)=1,Fm+1​(y,t)=(m​y−m+1)​Fm​(y,t)+y⁡(y+t−1)​∂yFm​(y,t).F_{1}(y,t)=1,\qquad F_{m+1}(y,t)=(my-m+1)F_{m}(y,t)+y(y+t-1)\partial_{y}F_{m}(y,t).

The deformation is designed so that the slice y=1y=1 recovers the original Poincaré polynomial:

Fm​(1,t)=Pm+1​(t).F_{m}(1,t)=P_{m+1}(t).

The derivative in the new direction recovers the convolution term in the recurrence:

∂yFm​(1,t)=Pm+1​(t)+Sm+2​(t),\partial_{y}F_{m}(1,t)=P_{m+1}(t)+S_{m+2}(t),

where

Sn​(t)=∑j=3n−2(n−2j−1)​Pj​(t)​Pn+1−j​(t).S_{n}(t)=\sum_{j=3}^{n-2}\binom{n-2}{j-1}P_{j}(t)P_{n+1-j}(t).

Thus the auxiliary variable yy is not decorative: it turns the nonlinear convolution in (3) into the slope of a moving zero curve.

Geometrically, for fixed t<0t<0 the positive roots of Fm​(y,t)F_{m}(y,t) lie in the interval 0<y<1−t0<y<1-t and are simple. As tt moves from 0−0^{-} to −∞-\infty, these roots move in ordered, noncolliding branches. Near t=0−t=0^{-} all positive branches lie below the horizontal line y=1y=1, while for t≪0t\ll 0 they all lie above it. Hence each branch crosses y=1y=1. The degree of Pm+1P_{m+1} leaves room for exactly one crossing per branch, and those crossings are precisely the roots of Pm+1P_{m+1}. The ordering of the branches then gives the sign alternation needed for interlacing. No monotonicity of the branches is assumed; the degree count is what rules out multiple crossings.

The deformation Fm​(y,t)F_{m}(y,t) is not a routine technical device: it is the key structural ingredient of the proof, converting the original recursion into a one-parameter family in which the move of real zeros can be controlled. Its discovery is a clear indication that the AI-assisted process reached beyond local symbolic manipulation and identified a genuinely new idea behind the theorem.

2. The recurrence and the Co-Math deformation

Recall that the polynomials Pn​(t)P_{n}(t) can be recursively computed by (2) and (3). For example, we have

P4​(t)=1+t,P5​(t)=1+5​t+t2,P6​(t)=1+16​t+16​t2+t3.P_{4}(t)=1+t,\ \ P_{5}(t)=1+5t+t^{2},\ \ \ P_{6}(t)=1+16t+16t^{2}+t^{3}.

By (1), it is obvious that Pn​(t)P_{n}(t) is monic of degree n−3n-3 and satisfies Pn​(0)=1P_{n}(0)=1. Put

(5) Sn​(t)=∑j=3n−2(n−2j−1)​Pj​(t)​Pn+1−j​(t)S_{n}(t)=\sum_{j=3}^{n-2}\binom{n-2}{j-1}P_{j}(t)P_{n+1-j}(t)

for n≥4n\geq 4, with the convention that an empty sum is zero.

The exponential generating function form of (3) will be used to identify the deformation. Define

(6) U⁡(x,t)=∑n≥3Pn​(t)​xn−1(n−1)!=x22!+(1+t)​x33!+(1+5​t+t2)​x44!+⋯.U(x,t)=\sum_{n\geq 3}P_{n}(t)\frac{x^{n-1}}{(n-1)!}=\frac{x^{2}}{2!}+(1+t)\frac{x^{3}}{3!}+(1+5t+t^{2})\frac{x^{4}}{4!}+\cdots.
Lemma 2.1.

The recurrence (3) is equivalent to

(7) ∂xU−x=(1+t)​U+t​U​∂xU.\partial_{x}U-x=(1+t)U+tU\partial_{x}U.

Moreover, (7) has a unique formal power-series solution in x2​ℚ​[t]​[[x]]x^{2}\mathbb{Q}[t][[x]].

Proof.

The coefficient of xn−2/(n−2)!x^{n-2}/(n-2)! in ∂xU\partial_{x}U is Pn​(t)P_{n}(t), and the coefficient of the same monomial in UU is Pn−1​(t)P_{n-1}(t). The coefficient of xn−2/(n−2)!x^{n-2}/(n-2)! in U​∂xUU\partial_{x}U is

∑j=3n−2(n−2j−1)​Pj​(t)​Pn+1−j​(t)=Sn​(t).\sum_{j=3}^{n-2}\binom{n-2}{j-1}P_{j}(t)P_{n+1-j}(t)=S_{n}(t).

The term −x-x removes the initial n=3n=3 coefficient. Thus the coefficient identity for n≥4n\geq 4 is exactly (3). Conversely, the same coefficient extraction recovers the recurrence. Since the coefficient of xn−1x^{n-1} in (7) is solved recursively from lower coefficients, the formal solution is unique. ∎

Now we define the bivariate deformation.

Definition 2.2.

Let F1​(y,t)=1F_{1}(y,t)=1, and for m≥1m\geq 1 set

(8) Fm+1​(y,t)=(m​y−m+1)​Fm​(y,t)+y⁡(y+t−1)​∂yFm​(y,t).F_{m+1}(y,t)=(my-m+1)F_{m}(y,t)+y(y+t-1)\partial_{y}F_{m}(y,t).

See §6 for geometric intuition behind this definition.

For example, we have

F2=y,F3=3​y2+(t−2)​y,F4=15​y3+10​(t−2)​y2+(t−2)​(t−3)​y.F_{2}=y,\qquad F_{3}=3y^{2}+(t-2)y,\qquad F_{4}=15y^{3}+10(t-2)y^{2}+(t-2)(t-3)y.

Let

(9) Φ⁡(x,y,t)=∑m≥1Fm​(y,t)​xmm!=x+x22!​y+x33!​(3​y2+(t−2)​y)+⋯.\Phi(x,y,t)=\sum_{m\geq 1}F_{m}(y,t)\frac{x^{m}}{m!}=x+\frac{x^{2}}{2!}y+\frac{x^{3}}{3!}\left(3y^{2}+(t-2)y\right)+\cdots.

Coefficient extraction from (8) gives the following linear PDE.

Lemma 2.3.

The series Φ\Phi uniquely satisfies

(10) (1−(y−1)​x)​∂xΦ−y⁡(y+t−1)​∂yΦ=1+Φ,Φ⁡(0,y,t)=0.\bigl(1-(y-1)x\bigr)\partial_{x}\Phi-y(y+t-1)\partial_{y}\Phi=1+\Phi,\qquad\Phi(0,y,t)=0.
Proof.

Since

∂xΦ=1+∑m≥1Fm+1​(y,t)​xmm!,\partial_{x}\Phi=1+\sum_{m\geq 1}F_{m+1}(y,t)\frac{x^{m}}{m!},

substituting (8) gives

∂xΦ=1+(y−1)​x​∂xΦ+Φ+y⁡(y+t−1)​∂yΦ,\partial_{x}\Phi=1+(y-1)x\partial_{x}\Phi+\Phi+y(y+t-1)\partial_{y}\Phi,

which is (10). Conversely, (10) implies (8) and thus follows the uniqueness. ∎

The next proposition is the algebraic bridge between the deformation and the original recurrence.

Proposition 2.4 (Slice and slope identities).

For all m≥1m\geq 1,

(11) Fm​(1,t)=Pm+1​(t).F_{m}(1,t)=P_{m+1}(t).

For all m≥2m\geq 2,

(12) ∂yFm​(1,t)=Pm+1​(t)+Sm+2​(t).\partial_{y}F_{m}(1,t)=P_{m+1}(t)+S_{m+2}(t).
Proof.

Let φ⁡(x,t)=Φ⁡(x,1,t)\varphi(x,t)=\Phi(x,1,t). We first identify φ\varphi. For fixed t≠0,1t\neq 0,1, we solve (10) by characteristics. The characteristic equations are

(13) d​xd​s=1−(y−1)​x,d​yd​s=−y⁡(y+t−1),d​td​s=0.\frac{dx}{ds}=1-(y-1)x,\qquad\frac{dy}{ds}=-y(y+t-1),\qquad\frac{dt}{ds}=0.

Start with the initial condition x⁡(0)=0x(0)=0. By (9), we have Φ⁡(0)=0\Phi(0)=0 and

d​Φd​s=d​xd​s​∂Φ∂x+d​yd​s​∂Φ∂y=1+Φ\frac{d\Phi}{ds}=\frac{dx}{ds}\frac{\partial\Phi}{\partial x}+\frac{dy}{ds}\frac{\partial\Phi}{\partial y}=1+\Phi

by (10). Thus letting u=esu=e^{s},

Φ=es−1=u−1.\Phi=e^{s}-1=u-1.

Let the integral curve (x⁡(s),y⁡(s))(x(s),y(s)) reach y=1y=1 at u=zu=z so that

φ=Φ|y=1=z−1.\varphi=\Phi|_{y=1}=z-1.

By Calculus, we can solve the differential equation for yy with y|u=z=1y|_{u=z}=1 to find

yy+t−1=1t​(zu)t−1.\frac{y}{y+t-1}=\frac{1}{t}\left(\frac{z}{u}\right)^{t-1}.

Substituting this expression into the linear equation

d​xd​u+y−1u​x=1u,x|u=1=0,\frac{dx}{du}+\frac{y-1}{u}x=\frac{1}{u},\qquad x|_{u=1}=0,

and integrating from u=1u=1 to u=zu=z after multiplying

exp⁡(∫y−1u​𝑑u)=zu​(t−(zu)t−1)\exp\left(\int\frac{y-1}{u}du\right)=\frac{z}{u}\left(t-\left(\frac{z}{u}\right)^{t-1}\right)

(14) φ=z−1,x=t2​(z−1)−zt+1t⁡(t−1).\varphi=z-1,\qquad x=\frac{t^{2}(z-1)-z^{t}+1}{t(t-1)}.

Here ztz^{t} is expanded as exp⁡(t​log⁡z)\exp(t\log z) near z=1z=1. The computation is an identity in ℚ​(t)​[[z−1]]\mathbb{Q}(t)[[z-1]]; after coefficient comparison, the resulting identities extend to all tt because both sides are polynomial in tt.

d​xd​z=t−zt−1t−1,d​Vd​x=zt−1−1t−zt−1.\frac{dx}{dz}=\frac{t-z^{t-1}}{t-1},\qquad\frac{dV}{dx}=\frac{z^{t-1}-1}{t-z^{t-1}}.

A direct substitution shows that VV satisfies

d​Vd​x−x=(1+t)​V+t​V​d​Vd​x,V∈x2​ℚ​[t]​[[x]].\frac{dV}{dx}-x=(1+t)V+tV\frac{dV}{dx},\qquad V\in x^{2}\mathbb{Q}[t][[x]].

(15) φ⁡(x,t)=x+U⁡(x,t).\varphi(x,t)=x+U(x,t).

Comparing coefficients in (15) gives (11). The identity was proved for generic tt, hence holds as a polynomial identity in tt.

It remains to identify the yy-slope. Evaluate (10) at y=1y=1:

∂xφ=1+φ+t​∂yΦ⁡(x,1,t).\partial_{x}\varphi=1+\varphi+t\partial_{y}\Phi(x,1,t).

Using φ=x+U\varphi=x+U and (7), we obtain

t​∂yΦ⁡(x,1,t)=∂xU−x−U=t⁡(U+U​∂xU).t\partial_{y}\Phi(x,1,t)=\partial_{x}U-x-U=t\bigl(U+U\partial_{x}U\bigr).

(16) ∂yΦ⁡(x,1,t)=U+U​∂xU.\partial_{y}\Phi(x,1,t)=U+U\partial_{x}U.

The coefficient of xm/m!x^{m}/m! in UU is Pm+1​(t)P_{m+1}(t) for m≥2m\geq 2, and the coefficient of xm/m!x^{m}/m! in U​∂xUU\partial_{x}U is Sm+2​(t)S_{m+2}(t). This proves (12). ∎

φ⁡(x,t)=x+∑m≥2xmm!​Pm+1​(t),x=t2​φ−(1+φ)t+1t⁡(t−1)\varphi(x,t)=x+\sum_{m\geq 2}\frac{x^{m}}{m!}P_{m+1}(t),\quad x=\frac{t^{2}\varphi-(1+\varphi)^{t}+1}{t(t-1)}

which is precisely Getzler’s formula in [Get95, p228].

3. A Sturm theorem for the deformation

We now study Fm​(y,t)F_{m}(y,t) as a polynomial in yy for fixed t<0t<0. Put

a=1−t>1.a=1-t>1.

Then y⁡(y+t−1)=y⁡(y−a)=−y⁡(a−y)y(y+t-1)=y(y-a)=-y(a-y).

Lemma 3.1.

For m≥1m\geq 1, Fm​(y,t)F_{m}(y,t) has degree m−1m-1 in yy and leading coefficient (2​m−3)!!(2m-3)!! for m≥2m\geq 2; for m=1m=1 the leading coefficient is 11. For m≥2m\geq 2 and t<0t<0, y=0y=0 is a simple root of Fm​(y,t)F_{m}(y,t).

Proof.

The degree and leading coefficient follow immediately from the recurrence: if the leading term of FmF_{m} is cm​ym−1c_{m}y^{m-1}, then the leading term of Fm+1F_{m+1} is

(m+(m−1))​cm​ym=(2​m−1)​cm​ym.\bigl(m+(m-1)\bigr)c_{m}y^{m}=(2m-1)c_{m}y^{m}.

Thus cm=(2​m−3)!!c_{m}=(2m-3)!! for m≥2m\geq 2.

For the root at zero, F2​(y,t)=yF_{2}(y,t)=y. If Fm​(y,t)=dm​(t)​y+O⁡(y2)F_{m}(y,t)=d_{m}(t)y+O(y^{2}), then (8) gives

Fm+1​(y,t)=dm​(t)​(t−m)​y+O⁡(y2).F_{m+1}(y,t)=d_{m}(t)(t-m)y+O(y^{2}).

Since t<0t<0, the factor t−mt-m is nonzero. Hence the root at 00 is simple for every m≥2m\geq 2. ∎

Proposition 3.2 (Fixed-tt root structure).

Fix t<0t<0 and m≥2m\geq 2. The polynomial Fm​(y,t)F_{m}(y,t) has the simple root y=0y=0 and exactly m−2m-2 further simple roots in the interval (0,1−t)(0,1-t). Consequently all roots of Fm​(y,t)F_{m}(y,t) are real and lie in [0,1−t)[0,1-t).

Proof.

We argue by induction on mm. The case m=2m=2 is F2=yF_{2}=y. Assume the claim for FmF_{m}. Let a=1−ta=1-t and define the positive weight

(17) wm​(y)=y(m−1)/a​(a−y)(1−m​t)/a,0<y<a.w_{m}(y)=y^{(m-1)/a}(a-y)^{(1-mt)/a},\qquad 0<y<a.

A direct logarithmic differentiation gives

in the open interval, in addition to the root at zero. The function wm​Fmw_{m}F_{m} vanishes at 00, at each rir_{i}, and at aa; the endpoint vanishing follows from the positive exponents in (17). Rolle’s theorem applied on the intervals

For later use we need the behavior of the positive roots as tt varies. By Proposition 3.2, the positive roots are simple for every t<0t<0, hence the implicit function theorem gives local real-analytic root branches. Since the roots are globally ordered and never collide, these local branches glue uniquely to continuous, indeed real-analytic, functions

(19) 0<r1(m)​(t)<r2(m)​(t)<⋯<rm−2(m)​(t)<1−t,t<0.0<r_{1}^{(m)}(t)<r_{2}^{(m)}(t)<\cdots<r_{m-2}^{(m)}(t)<1-t,\qquad t<0.

Lemma 3.3 (Behavior near t=0t=0).

For fixed m≥2m\geq 2, all positive roots ri(m)​(t)r_{i}^{(m)}(t) lie below 11 for all sufficiently small negative tt.

Proof.

Suppose not. Then there are tk→0−t_{k}\to 0^{-} and positive roots rik(m)​(tk)r_{i_{k}}^{(m)}(t_{k}) with rik(m)​(tk)≥1r_{i_{k}}^{(m)}(t_{k})\geq 1. To analyze the other end, scale yy by tt. Define

(20) Hm,t​(x)=t−(m−1)​Fm​(t​x,t).H_{m,t}(x)=t^{-(m-1)}F_{m}(tx,t).

Hence, as t→−∞t\to-\infty, these polynomials converge coefficientwise to polynomials Gm​(x)G_{m}(x) determined by

(21) G1​(x)=1,Gm+1​(x)=m​x​Gm​(x)+x⁡(x+1)​Gm′​(x).G_{1}(x)=1,\qquad G_{m+1}(x)=mxG_{m}(x)+x(x+1)G_{m}^{\prime}(x).
Lemma 3.4.

For m≥2m\geq 2, Gm​(x)G_{m}(x) has a simple root at x=0x=0 and exactly m−2m-2 further simple roots in (−1,0)(-1,0).

Proof.

The proof is the limiting analogue of Proposition 3.2. The case m=2m=2 is G2=xG_{2}=x. Assume the result for GmG_{m}. On (−1,0)(-1,0) set vm​(x)=(1+x)mv_{m}(x)=(1+x)^{m}. Then

(22) dd​x​(vm​(x)​Gm​(x))=vm​(x)x⁡(1+x)​Gm+1​(x).\frac{d}{dx}\bigl(v_{m}(x)G_{m}(x)\bigr)=\frac{v_{m}(x)}{x(1+x)}G_{m+1}(x).

Lemma 3.5 (Behavior as t→−∞t\to-\infty).

For fixed m≥2m\geq 2, every positive root ri(m)​(t)r_{i}^{(m)}(t) tends to +∞+\infty as t→−∞t\to-\infty. In particular, all positive roots lie above 11 for all sufficiently negative tt.

for some αi∈(−1,0)\alpha_{i}\in(-1,0). Since t→−∞t\to-\infty, this implies ri(m)​(t)→+∞r_{i}^{(m)}(t)\to+\infty. ∎

4. Proof of real-rootedness and interlacing

We now prove the main theorem. Fix n≥4n\geq 4 and put

m=n−1,d=n−3=m−2.m=n-1,\qquad d=n-3=m-2.

Besides the trivial root y=0y=0, the polynomial Fm​(y,t)F_{m}(y,t) has d=m−2d=m-2 positive root branches

0<r1​(t)<⋯<rd​(t)<1−t.0<r_{1}(t)<\cdots<r_{d}(t)<1-t.

Only these positive branches are relevant for the crossing argument, since the trivial branch y=0y=0 never intersects the slice y=1y=1. By Lemma 3.3, all ri​(t)r_{i}(t) are below 11 when tt is close to 0−0^{-}. By Lemma 3.5, all ri​(t)r_{i}(t) are above 11 for t≪0t\ll 0. Continuity of the ordered roots therefore implies that each branch crosses the horizontal line y=1y=1 at least once. This step uses no monotonicity of the branch in tt. By Proposition 2.4, these crossings are exactly the zeros of

Fm​(1,t)=Pm+1​(t)=Pn​(t).F_{m}(1,t)=P_{m+1}(t)=P_{n}(t).

By (1), PnP_{n} has degree dd. Since there are dd branches and each branch crosses at least once, there can be exactly one crossing on each branch and no other zeros. Hence PnP_{n} has d=n−3d=n-3 distinct roots, all lying in (−∞,0)(-\infty,0). This proves Theorem 1.1.

It remains to record the interlacing, which follows from the same geometry. Let τi\tau_{i} be the unique crossing time of the branch rir_{i}, so that

ri​(τi)=1,Pn​(τi)=0.r_{i}(\tau_{i})=1,\qquad P_{n}(\tau_{i})=0.

The branch ordering implies

(23) τ1<τ2<⋯<τd<0.\tau_{1}<\tau_{2}<\cdots<\tau_{d}<0.

Indeed, at time τi\tau_{i} the branch rjr_{j} with j>ij>i lies above 11, and since it is below 11 near 0−0^{-} and crosses only once, its crossing time must be larger than τi\tau_{i}.

At t=τit=\tau_{i}, factor FmF_{m} as a polynomial in yy:

(24) Fm​(y,τi)=cm​y​∏k=1d(y−rk​(τi)),cm=(2​m−3)!!>0.F_{m}(y,\tau_{i})=c_{m}\,y\prod_{k=1}^{d}\bigl(y-r_{k}(\tau_{i})\bigr),\qquad c_{m}=(2m-3)!!>0.

Since ri​(τi)=1r_{i}(\tau_{i})=1, the lower branches satisfy rk​(τi)<1r_{k}(\tau_{i})<1 for k<ik<i, while the upper branches satisfy rk​(τi)>1r_{k}(\tau_{i})>1 for k>ik>i. Thus

(25) sgn∂yFm(1,τi)=(−1)d−i.\operatorname{sgn}\,\partial_{y}F_{m}(1,\tau_{i})=(-1)^{d-i}.

Using the slope identity (12) with m=n−1m=n-1 gives

∂yFn−1​(1,t)=Pn​(t)+Sn+1​(t).\partial_{y}F_{n-1}(1,t)=P_{n}(t)+S_{n+1}(t).

At a zero τi\tau_{i} of PnP_{n}, this becomes

(26) Sn+1​(τi)=∂yFn−1​(1,τi),S_{n+1}(\tau_{i})=\partial_{y}F_{n-1}(1,\tau_{i}),

so Sn+1​(τi)S_{n+1}(\tau_{i}) has the sign in (25). The recurrence for Pn+1P_{n+1} gives

(27) Pn+1​(τi)=τi​Sn+1​(τi).P_{n+1}(\tau_{i})=\tau_{i}S_{n+1}(\tau_{i}).

Since τi<0\tau_{i}<0, the signs of Pn+1​(τi)P_{n+1}(\tau_{i}) alternate as ii varies. Therefore Pn+1P_{n+1} has a root in each interval (τi,τi+1)(\tau_{i},\tau_{i+1}).

There is also a root on each side. At the right end, Pn+1​(τd)<0P_{n+1}(\tau_{d})<0 by (25)–(27), while Pn+1​(0)=1P_{n+1}(0)=1, so there is a root in (τd,0)(\tau_{d},0). At the left end, Pn+1P_{n+1} is monic of degree d+1d+1, hence

sgn⁡Pn+1​(t)=(−1)d+1(t≪0),\operatorname{sgn}P_{n+1}(t)=(-1)^{d+1}\qquad(t\ll 0),

whereas Pn+1​(τ1)P_{n+1}(\tau_{1}) has sign (−1)d(-1)^{d}. Hence there is a root in (−∞,τ1)(-\infty,\tau_{1}). We have found d+1=deg⁡Pn+1d+1=\deg P_{n+1} distinct real roots, with exactly one in each interval. This proves Theorem 1.2.

Corollary 4.1.

For every n≥3n\geq 3, the Betti number sequence

bn,0,bn,1,…,bn,n−3b_{n,0},b_{n,1},\ldots,b_{n,n-3}

of ℳ¯0,n\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n} is ultra-log-concave:

(bn,i(n−3i))2≥bn,i−1(n−3i−1)​bn,i+1(n−3i+1)(1≤i≤n−4).\left(\frac{b_{n,i}}{\binom{n-3}{i}}\right)^{2}\geq\frac{b_{n,i-1}}{\binom{n-3}{i-1}}\frac{b_{n,i+1}}{\binom{n-3}{i+1}}\qquad(1\leq i\leq n-4).
Proof.

The coefficients of PnP_{n} are nonnegative, either by their cohomological meaning or directly from the recurrence. The ultra-log-concavity follows directly from the real-rootedness together with Newton’s inequalities. ∎

Remark 4.2 (Higher ultra-log-concavities).

A sequence of positive integers

a0,a1,⋯,ana_{0},a_{1},\cdots,a_{n}

is called rr-ultra-log-concave (r-ULC for short) if

(ai(ni)r)2≥ai−1(ni−1)r​ai+1(ni+1)r(1≤i≤n−1).\left(\frac{a_{i}}{\binom{n}{i}^{r}}\right)^{2}\geq\frac{a_{i-1}}{\binom{n}{i-1}^{r}}\frac{a_{i+1}}{\binom{n}{i+1}^{r}}\qquad(1\leq i\leq n-1).

It is obvious that rr-ULC implies (r−1)(r-1)-ULC for r≥1r\geq 1 and 00-ULC is the ordinary log-concavity. Based on numerical computations, we expect that the Betti sequence {bn,i| 0≤i≤n−3}\{b_{n,i}\,|\,0\leq i\leq n-3\} is in fact 22-ULC. Furthermore, it was proved in [CK26, Corollary 3.4] that the Betti sequence is asymptotically 33-ULC but not 44-ULC. As the roots of a polynomial determine the coefficients, these higher ULCs indicate that the locations of zeros of Pn​(t)P_{n}(t) may have certain patterns which warrant further investigations.

Remark 4.3 (Refined log-concavities).

The log-concavity in Corollary 4.1 can be refined by considering the action of the symmetric group SnS_{n} on ℳ¯0,n\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n} by permuting the marked points. For each 0≤i≤n−30\leq i\leq n-3, we can decompose the SnS_{n}-module H2​i​(ℳ¯0,n)H^{2i}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n}) into a direct sum of irreducible representations and ask whether the multiplicities multλ​H2​i​(ℳ¯0,n)\mathrm{mult}_{\lambda}H^{2i}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n}) of an irreducible representation λ\lambda of SnS_{n} form a log-concave sequence or not (cf. [CKL24, Conjecture 1.6]).

Of particular interest is the invariant part

H2​k​(ℳ¯0,n)Sn=H2​k​(ℳ¯0,n/Sn)H^{2k}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n})^{S_{n}}=H^{2k}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n}/S_{n})

which is the cohomology of the moduli space ℳ¯0,n/Sn\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n}/S_{n} of stable curves of genus 0 with nn unordered marked points. It was proved in [CKL24, Corollary 6.10 and Corollary 6.11] that the Betti sequence of ℳ¯0,n/Sn\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n}/S_{n} is asymptotically log-concave but not ultra-log-concave. In particular, the Poincaré polynomial of ℳ¯0,n/Sn\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n}/S_{n} is not real-rooted. This indicates that a new approach is required for refined log-concavities.

5. Fulton–MacPherson compactification of the configuration space

A closely related space to ℳ¯0,n\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n} is the Fulton–MacPherson compactification ℙ1​[n]\mathbb{P}^{1}[n] (FM space for short) of the configuration space

(ℙ1)n−Δ,Δ=⋃i≠jΔi​j(\mathbb{P}^{1})^{n}-\Delta,\qquad\Delta=\bigcup_{i\neq j}\Delta_{ij}

of nn ordered distinct points in the projective line ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} where Δi​j\Delta_{ij} denotes the locus where iith and jjth points coincide. See [FM94] and [Man99, §4.3]. The FM space ℙ1​[n]\mathbb{P}^{1}[n] is the wonderful compactification of the configuration space which is obtained by a sequence of blow-ups from (ℙ1)n(\mathbb{P}^{1})^{n} and is isomorphic to the moduli space of stable maps to ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} of degree 1:

ℙ1​[n]≅ℳ¯0,n​(ℙ1,1).\mathbb{P}^{1}[n]\cong\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n}(\mathbb{P}^{1},1).

There is a canonical choice of an ample line bundle and ℳ¯0,n\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n} is the geometric invariant theory quotient of ℙ1​[n]\mathbb{P}^{1}[n] by the action of Aut⁡(ℙ1)\mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb{P}^{1}).

By construction, ℙ1​[n]\mathbb{P}^{1}[n] is a smooth projective variety of dimension nn with vanishing odd cohomology and its Betti sequence

b~n,i=dimH2​i​(ℙ1​[n])(0≤i≤n)\tilde{b}_{n,i}=\dim H^{2i}(\mathbb{P}^{1}[n])\qquad(0\leq i\leq n)

is unimodal and palindromic.

By the same technique we used for ℳ¯0,n\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n}, we obtain the following.

Theorem 5.1.

The Poincaré polynomial P~n​(t)=∑ib~n,i​ti\widetilde{P}_{n}(t)=\sum_{i}\tilde{b}_{n,i}t^{i} of ℙ1​[n]\mathbb{P}^{1}[n] has only negative real roots for n≥1n\geq 1.

Proof.

Since the proof parallels that of Theorem 1.1, we only provide an outline here. Let

φ⁡(x,t)=∑m≥1xmm!​Pm+1​(t),ψ⁡(x,t)=1+∑n≥1xnn!​P~n​(t).\varphi(x,t)=\sum_{m\geq 1}\frac{x^{m}}{m!}P_{m+1}(t),\quad\psi(x,t)=1+\sum_{n\geq 1}\frac{x^{n}}{n!}\widetilde{P}_{n}(t).

Then by [Man99, IV. (4.24)], we have

ψ=(1+φ)t+1\psi=(1+\varphi)^{t+1}

which is equivalent to the formula (cf. [CK26, §4])

(28) P~n​(t)=∑j=0n(nj)​tmin⁡{n−j,2}​Pj+1​(t)​Pn+1−j​(t)\widetilde{P}_{n}(t)=\sum_{j=0}^{n}\binom{n}{j}t^{\min\{n-j,2\}}P_{j+1}(t)P_{n+1-j}(t)

with the convention P1=P2=1P_{1}=P_{2}=1. Geometrically, (28) is a direct consequence of the wall crossings of moduli spaces of δ\delta-stable maps to the quotient stack [ℂ2/ℂ∗][\mathbb{C}^{2}/\mathbb{C}^{*}] (cf. [CKL23, §6.2]).

The deformations F~n​(y,t)\widetilde{F}_{n}(y,t) and Ψ⁡(x,y,t)\Psi(x,y,t) of P~n​(t)\widetilde{P}_{n}(t) and ψ⁡(x,t)\psi(x,t) respectively are defined by

Ψ⁡(x,y,t)=(1+Φ⁡(x,y,t))t+1=1+∑n≥1xnn!​F~n​(y,t)\Psi(x,y,t)=(1+\Phi(x,y,t))^{t+1}=1+\sum_{n\geq 1}\frac{x^{n}}{n!}\widetilde{F}_{n}(y,t)

using the deformation (9) of φ\varphi.

The coefficients F~n​(y,t)\widetilde{F}_{n}(y,t) are all divisible by t+1t+1. Indeed,

(1+Φ)t+1−1=∑k≥1(t+1k)​Φk,(1+\Phi)^{t+1}-1=\sum_{k\geq 1}\binom{t+1}{k}\Phi^{k},

and each binomial coefficient (t+1k)=(t+1)t(t−1)⋯(t−k+2)k!\binom{t+1}{k}=\frac{(t+1)t(t-1)\cdots(t-k+2)}{k!} contains the factor t+1t+1. Thus the zero locus of F~n\widetilde{F}_{n} contains the extraneous vertical component t=−1t=-1. We remove this common component and work with the residual deformation

F^n​(y,t):=F~n​(y,t)t+1.\widehat{F}_{n}(y,t):=\frac{\widetilde{F}_{n}(y,t)}{t+1}.

Equivalently,

Ψ^​(x,y,t):=(1+Φ⁡(x,y,t))t+1−1t+1=∑n≥1F^n​(y,t)​xnn!.\widehat{\Psi}(x,y,t):=\frac{(1+\Phi(x,y,t))^{t+1}-1}{t+1}=\sum_{n\geq 1}\widehat{F}_{n}(y,t)\frac{x^{n}}{n!}.

On the slice y=1y=1, this gives

F^n​(1,t)=P^n​(t),P^n​(t):=P~n​(t)t+1.\widehat{F}_{n}(1,t)=\widehat{P}_{n}(t),\qquad\widehat{P}_{n}(t):=\frac{\widetilde{P}_{n}(t)}{t+1}.

Thus it suffices to prove that P^n​(t)\widehat{P}_{n}(t) has only negative real roots; the removed factor t+1t+1 then contributes the additional root t=−1t=-1 of P~n​(t)\widetilde{P}_{n}(t).

We next record the recurrence satisfied by the residual deformation. Since Ψ=(1+Φ)t+1\Psi=(1+\Phi)^{t+1} and Φ\Phi satisfies

(1−(y−1)​x)​∂xΦ−y⁡(y+t−1)​∂yΦ=1+Φ,\bigl(1-(y-1)x\bigr)\partial_{x}\Phi-y(y+t-1)\partial_{y}\Phi=1+\Phi,

we get

(1−(y−1)​x)​∂xΨ−y⁡(y+t−1)​∂yΨ=(t+1)​Ψ.\bigl(1-(y-1)x\bigr)\partial_{x}\Psi-y(y+t-1)\partial_{y}\Psi=(t+1)\Psi.

Comparing coefficients and dividing by t+1t+1, the polynomials F^n\widehat{F}_{n} satisfy

(29) F^n+1​(y,t)=(n​y−n+t+1)​F^n​(y,t)+y⁡(y+t−1)​∂yF^n​(y,t),F^1​(y,t)=1.\widehat{F}_{n+1}(y,t)=(ny-n+t+1)\widehat{F}_{n}(y,t)+y(y+t-1)\partial_{y}\widehat{F}_{n}(y,t),\qquad\widehat{F}_{1}(y,t)=1.

Fix t<0t<0, and put a=1−ta=1-t. Then (29) becomes

F^n+1=(n​y−n+2−a)​F^n−y⁡(a−y)​∂yF^n.\widehat{F}_{n+1}=(ny-n+2-a)\widehat{F}_{n}-y(a-y)\partial_{y}\widehat{F}_{n}.

For 0<y<a0<y<a, define

wn​(y)=yαn​(a−y)βn,αn=n+a−2a,βn=(n−1)​a−n+2a.w_{n}(y)=y^{\alpha_{n}}(a-y)^{\beta_{n}},\qquad\alpha_{n}=\frac{n+a-2}{a},\qquad\beta_{n}=\frac{(n-1)a-n+2}{a}.

Both exponents are positive. A direct calculation gives the Sturm identity

(30) dd​y​(wn​(y)​F^n​(y,t))=−wn​(y)y⁡(a−y)​F^n+1​(y,t),\frac{d}{dy}\bigl(w_{n}(y)\widehat{F}_{n}(y,t)\bigr)=-\frac{w_{n}(y)}{y(a-y)}\widehat{F}_{n+1}(y,t),

exactly as in the proof of the Sturm theorem for Fm​(y,t)F_{m}(y,t), Rolle’s theorem applied to (30) shows by induction that, for every t<0t<0, the polynomial F^n​(⋅,t)\widehat{F}_{n}(\,\cdot\,,t) has n−1n-1 simple roots, all lying in the interval 0<y<1−t0<y<1-t. We denote them by

0<r1​(t)<⋯<rn−1​(t)<1−t.0<r_{1}(t)<\cdots<r_{n-1}(t)<1-t.

Since the roots are simple, these ordered roots depend continuously on t<0t<0. The recurrence also shows inductively that degy⁡F^n=n−1\deg_{y}\widehat{F}_{n}=n-1 and that the leading coefficient is (2​n−3)!!>0(2n-3)!!>0 for n≥2n\geq 2.

It remains to compare the branches ri​(t)r_{i}(t) with the slice y=1y=1. First, as t→0−t\to 0^{-}, no branch can stay at or above y=1y=1. Otherwise, after passing to a subsequence, one would obtain a limiting zero of F^n​(y,0)\widehat{F}_{n}(y,0) at y=1y=1. But

F^n​(1,0)=P^n​(0)=1,\widehat{F}_{n}(1,0)=\widehat{P}_{n}(0)=1,

a contradiction. Hence all branches lie below y=1y=1 for t<0t<0 sufficiently close to 00.

Second, as t→−∞t\to-\infty, all branches go to +∞+\infty. This follows by the same scaling argument used earlier. Namely, define

Hn,t​(x)=t−(n−1)​F^n​(t​x,t).H_{n,t}(x)=t^{-(n-1)}\widehat{F}_{n}(tx,t).

Then Hn,tH_{n,t} converges coefficientwise to the polynomial Kn​(x)K_{n}(x) defined by

K1​(x)=1,Kn+1​(x)=(n​x+1)​Kn​(x)+x⁡(x+1)​Kn′​(x).K_{1}(x)=1,\qquad K_{n+1}(x)=(nx+1)K_{n}(x)+x(x+1)K_{n}^{\prime}(x).

For n≥2n\geq 2, the same Sturm–Rolle argument on (−1,0)(-1,0) shows that KnK_{n} has n−1n-1 simple roots in [−1,0)[-1,0), one at −1-1 and the remaining n−2n-2 in (−1,0)(-1,0). Hence the roots of Hn,tH_{n,t} converge to negative limits, and therefore the corresponding positive roots ri​(t)r_{i}(t) of F^n​(y,t)\widehat{F}_{n}(y,t) tend to +∞+\infty as t→−∞t\to-\infty.

Thus each continuous branch ri​(t)r_{i}(t) lies below y=1y=1 near t=0−t=0^{-} and above y=1y=1 for t≪0t\ll 0. Therefore each branch crosses the slice y=1y=1 at least once. These crossing times are exactly the zeros of

F^n​(1,t)=P^n​(t).\widehat{F}_{n}(1,t)=\widehat{P}_{n}(t).

Moreover, at a fixed t<0t<0, the roots of F^n​(⋅,t)\widehat{F}_{n}(\,\cdot\,,t) are simple and distinct, so two different branches cannot cross y=1y=1 at the same time.

Consequently P^n​(t)\widehat{P}_{n}(t) has at least n−1n-1 distinct negative real roots. Since ℙ1​[n]\mathbb{P}^{1}[n] is smooth projective of dimension nn, P~n​(t)\widetilde{P}_{n}(t) has degree nn and leading coefficient 11. Therefore P^n​(t)=P~n​(t)t+1\widehat{P}_{n}(t)=\frac{\widetilde{P}_{n}(t)}{t+1} has degree n−1n-1. The n−1n-1 negative roots found above are all its roots. Finally, the removed factor t+1t+1 contributes the additional negative root t=−1t=-1. Hence P~n​(t)\widetilde{P}_{n}(t) has only negative real roots. ∎

By Newton’s inequalities again, we have the following.

Corollary 5.2.

The Betti sequence {b~n,i}0≤i≤n\{\tilde{b}_{n,i}\}_{0\leq i\leq n} of ℙ1​[n]\mathbb{P}^{1}[n] is ultra-log-concave.

By [CK26, Corollary 4.2], the Betti sequence is asymptotically 3-ULC.

6. Geometric intuition for the deformation Fm​(y,t)F_{m}(y,t)

The key structural idea of the proof was to replace the one-variable nonlinear recurrence for the Poincaré polynomials Pn​(t)P_{n}(t) by a two-variable deformation Fm​(y,t)F_{m}(y,t) whose geometry is much more rigid. Writing m=n−1m=n-1, we introduced polynomials Fm​(y,t)F_{m}(y,t) satisfying

Fm​(1,t)=Pm+1​(t).F_{m}(1,t)=P_{m+1}(t).

Thus the original Poincaré polynomial is recovered as the slice of the deformation along the hyperplane y=1y=1, see Figure 1.

The point of this construction is that the variable yy is not merely an auxiliary parameter: it is chosen so that the recurrence in mm becomes a first-order differential recurrence in the yy-direction,

Fm+1​(y,t)=(m​y−m+1)​Fm​(y,t)+y⁡(y+t−1)​∂yFm​(y,t).F_{m+1}(y,t)=(my-m+1)F_{m}(y,t)+y(y+t-1)\,\partial_{y}F_{m}(y,t).

From the point of view of analysis, this is a transport-type evolution in the yy-variable. The coefficient y⁡(y+t−1)y(y+t-1) is the decisive feature that anchors a Sturm problem on the interval 0<y<1−t0<y<1-t. For t<0t<0, writing a=1−t>1a=1-t>1, one has

y⁡(y+t−1)=y⁡(y−a)=−y⁡(a−y),y(y+t-1)=y(y-a)=-\,y(a-y),

so the derivative term vanishes exactly at the two boundary points

y=0,y=a=1−t.y=0,\qquad y=a=1-t.

This singles out the interval 0≤y≤1−t0\leq y\leq 1-t as the natural geometric domain for the zero set of Fm​(⋅,t)F_{m}(\,\cdot\,,t). The conceptual gain is that, for fixed t<0t<0, the recurrence may be rewritten in Sturm form. After multiplication by a suitable positive weight wm​(y)w_{m}(y), one obtains an identity of the shape

dd​y​(wm​(y)​Fm​(y,t))=−wm​(y)y⁡(1−t−y)​Fm+1​(y,t).\frac{d}{dy}\bigl(w_{m}(y)F_{m}(y,t)\bigr)=-\frac{w_{m}(y)}{y(1-t-y)}\,F_{m+1}(y,t).

Hence the zeros of Fm+1​(⋅,t)F_{m+1}(\,\cdot\,,t) are the critical points of wm​Fmw_{m}F_{m}. Rolle’s theorem then forces the roots of Fm+1F_{m+1} to appear between the roots of FmF_{m}, with the endpoints y=0y=0 and y=1−ty=1-t providing the extra control needed to close the induction. In this way the deformation turns the original problem into a Sturm-chain argument in the auxiliary variable yy.

7. Overview of the Co-Math proof development

The proof above emerged from an iterative Co-Math process rather than from a single polished answer. The progression is instructive because it shows both the power and the risks of agentic mathematical collaboration.

The first attempts already found the main architecture: reduce the problem to interlacing, introduce a bivariate deformation, study its roots by a Rolle-theoretic argument, and interpret the roots of PnP_{n} as crossings of positive yy-root branches through the line y=1y=1. At that stage, however, several crucial details were still heuristic. The derivation of the FmF_{m}-recurrence was not fully justified, the branch-crossing argument assumed monotonicity that had not been proved, and the endpoint behavior as t→0−t\to 0^{-} and t→−∞t\to-\infty was only partially controlled.

The next round strengthened the algebra. The generating function (7), the PDE (10), and the slice identity Fm​(1,t)=Pm+1​(t)F_{m}(1,t)=P_{m+1}(t) were made explicit. The fixed-tt root structure was converted into the weighted derivative identity (18), so Rolle’s theorem could be applied without hidden assumptions. Computation was useful in this stage, but only as a guardrail: it checked indexing, small cases, and the identities involving Fm​(1,t)F_{m}(1,t) and ∂yFm​(1,t)\partial_{y}F_{m}(1,t). It did not prove the analytic branch argument.

The final step replaced the remaining experimental and computation-based claims by proof. A possible topological zigzag problem for root branches was eliminated by a degree count: each branch must cross y=1y=1 at least once, while Pn​(t)=Fn−1​(1,t)P_{n}(t)=F_{n-1}(1,t) has exactly as many possible zeros as there are branches. The behavior at t→−∞t\to-\infty was justified by the scaled limit Hm,t→GmH_{m,t}\to G_{m} and the independent Sturm analysis of GmG_{m} on (−1,0)(-1,0). This turned the geometric picture into a rigorous crossing theorem and then into strict interlacing.

Our workflow aligns closely with the design principles described in the AI co-mathematician paper of Zheng et al. [ZvGZ+26]: the system supported iterative refinement, numerical exploration, proof development, and production of native mathematical artifacts. It also illustrates the paper’s cautions. Early drafts were written in confident LaTeX even when some lemmas were not yet proved; the bibliography changed across attempts, and key provenance information, such as the Keel–Manin–Getzler origin of the recurrence and the relevant work of Choi–Kiem–Lee, was not preserved consistently.

A stronger agentic workflow should maintain a persistent gap registry, a computation log indicating exactly what was checked and the exact ranges verified, and a reference manifest distinguishing sources used in the proof from background literature. In this problem, the most productive and interesting behavior was not one-shot theorem proving but the ability to keep a promising architecture alive, accept finite computation as provisional evidence, and gradually replace it with exact lemmas. The point is not that computation was used as proof, but that it was used as a temporary scaffold for proof discovery. For instance, the identities

Fm​(1,t)=Pm+1​(t),∂yFm​(1,t)=Pm+1​(t)+Sm+2​(t),F_{m}(1,t)=P_{m+1}(t),\qquad\partial_{y}F_{m}(1,t)=P_{m+1}(t)+S_{m+2}(t),

together with the observed real-rootedness and branch-crossing behavior of Fm​(y,t)F_{m}(y,t), were first supported by finite symbolic and numerical checks. Those checks were strong enough for the system to preserve the bivariate deformation as the central proof architecture, even while several steps remained unproved. Later iterations then discharged the gaps: the identities were derived from the generating-function PDE, the root structure was proved by a Sturm–Rolle argument, and the endpoint behavior of the moving branches was proved. This illustrates a genuine strength of the Co-Mathematician workflow: it can reason provisionally from well-documented computational evidence without confusing that evidence with the final proof.
